meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 79fe18157a1d, papers/coupled-spring). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them.

topics.name: Potential and its minimum
topics.description: The potential $U(x)=x_0^2+x_0x_1+x_1^2$ is studied through local and global minimum arguments at the origin.

topics.name: Analytic minimum test
topics.description: Analyticity, a zero gradient and a positive definite Hessian give a local minimum.

topics.name: Analyticity and derivatives
topics.description: The polynomial $U$ has a zero gradient at the origin and a constant positive definite Hessian.

topics.name: Quadratic lower bound
topics.description: Positive definiteness gives a positive lower bound proportional to the squared norm in finite dimensions.

topics.name: Taylor remainder
topics.description: The Taylor remainder becomes small enough for the quadratic term to control the change in the function.

topics.name: Cubic local minimum
topics.description: Adding $x_0^3$ preserves the gradient and Hessian at the origin, so the local minimum persists.

topics.name: Failure of global minimality
topics.description: The cubic perturbation takes values below its value at the origin away from the local minimum.

topics.name: The smoothness assumption
topics.description: The page identifies a use of smoothness that can be avoided by keeping an earlier quadratic lower bound.

topics.name: Polar form and symmetry
topics.description: The polar form sums the second derivative in both orders, and symmetry makes half that sum equal to the Hessian.

notes.coercive_of_posdef: On a finite-dimensional real normed space, positivity of $D^2f(a)[h,h]$ for every nonzero $h$ gives some $C>0$ with $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$ for all $h$. The formal statement requires neither analyticity, a zero gradient nor a separate smoothness assumption. Its conclusion is a bound on the Hessian, not yet a minimum of $f$.
notes.coercive_of_posdef_of_contdiff: For a real-valued function on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the formal statement assumes smoothness of all orders at $a$ and positivity of $D^2f(a)[h,h]$ for nonzero $h$. It gives some $C>0$ with $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$ for every $h$. The proof uses smoothness to obtain Hessian symmetry.
notes.coupled_spring_potential: There is a neighbourhood of the origin on which $U(0)\le U(x)$. The formal statement gives this non-strict local inequality. It does not state strictness away from the origin, uniqueness or a global inequality. The page presents those further conclusions separately through the completed-square argument and supplementary proofs.
notes.couplingPotential: The formal definition assigns $U(x)=x_0^2+x_0x_1+x_1^2$ to every point of the real plane. It contains no spring constant, mass or equation of motion. Those quantities belong to the mechanical interpretation later in the page, where the physical potential energy is $kU(x)$.
notes.couplingPotential_analyticAt: The potential $U$ is analytic at every point of the real plane. The source obtains this from the coordinate functions by taking squares, a product and sums, matching the polynomial formula. No restriction to the origin and no hypothesis about a displacement being small appear in the formal statement.
notes.couplingPotential_gradient_zero: The formal statement is $\nabla U(0)=0$. Its proof uses the derivative formula and the correspondence between a derivative and a gradient in the Euclidean plane. This establishes the critical-point hypothesis for the minimum test; it does not by itself classify the critical point as a minimum.
notes.couplingPotential_hasFDerivAt: At an arbitrary point $x$, the derivative sends an increment $h$ to $(2x_0+x_1)h_0+(x_0+2x_1)h_1$. The formal statement identifies this linear functional as the derivative of $U$. It is the derivative on the whole real plane; the vanishing of its coefficients at the origin is established separately.
notes.couplingPotential_iteratedFDeriv_two: For every base point $z$ and vectors $u,v$, the formal statement gives $D^2U(z)[u,v]=2u_0v_0+u_0v_1+u_1v_0+2u_1v_1$. These four coefficients are the entries of $K$. The formula is independent of $z$ and allows distinct vectors in the two positions, so it specifies the full Hessian rather than only its diagonal values.
notes.couplingPotential_posDef: The formal statement gives $D^2U(0)[h,h]>0$ for every nonzero vector $h$. The proof substitutes the explicit Hessian formula and uses nonnegativity of squares. It supplies the positivity hypothesis for the analytic test. The numerical estimate $D^2U(0)[h,h]\ge\lVert h\rVert^2$ appears in the page but is not the conclusion of this theorem.
notes.isLocalMin.of_subsingleton: If a topological space has at most one point, every real-valued function has a local minimum at each point of that space. No differentiability or vector-space hypothesis is needed. The zero-dimensional vector space in the page is an instance of this statement, allowing the analytic test to handle that case separately.
notes.isLocalMin_of_posDef_of_littleo: The formal statement assumes a finite-dimensional real inner product space, a quadratic Taylor remainder $o(\lVert x-a\rVert^2)$, zero gradient, smoothness of all orders at $a$, and a positive definite Hessian there. It concludes a local minimum. The proof obtains the lower bound twice and uses smoothness in the second call; the page argues that this second call can be omitted.
notes.iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap: The formal definition is $Q(h)=D^2f(a)[h,h]$. It establishes the quadratic dependence on $h$ and the identity relating $Q(u+v)$ to $Q(u)$, $Q(v)$ and the associated polar form. This construction alone assumes neither analyticity nor positive definiteness; those are separate hypotheses in the subsequent minimum test.
notes.iteratedFDeriv_two_swap: The formal statement assumes that $f$ is smooth of all orders at $a$ in a real normed space. It concludes $D^2f(a)[u,v]=D^2f(a)[v,u]$ for every pair of vectors. This symmetry is the step used to identify half the polar form with the Hessian in the lower-bound proof that assumes smoothness.
notes.le_of_littleO: Fix $x$ and write $h=x-a$. The formal statement assumes $D^2f(a)[h,h]\ge C\lVert h\rVert^2$, $Df(a)[h]=0$, and $|f(x)-f(a)-Df(a)[h]-\tfrac12D^2f(a)[h,h]|\le\tfrac C2\lVert h\rVert^2$. It concludes $f(a)\le f(x)$. This is a pointwise implication; it neither chooses a neighbourhood nor assumes a little-o estimate itself. No finite-dimensional assumption is imposed.
notes.littleO_of_powerseries: If $f$ agrees with a convergent power series on a ball of positive radius around $a$, the formal statement gives a remainder $o(\lVert x-a\rVert^2)$ after subtracting the terms of degrees zero, one and two. It works on a real normed space without requiring finite dimensionality or a zero gradient; the linear term vanishes only at a critical point.
notes.polarBilin_iteratedFDerivQuadraticMap: With $B(u,v)=D^2f(a)[u,v]$ and $Q(h)=B(h,h)$, the formal statement is $Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)=B(u,v)+B(v,u)$. No smoothness assumption is needed for this identity on a real normed space. It gives the sum of the two orders; identifying half that sum with $B$ off the diagonal additionally requires symmetry.
notes.second_derivative_test: Let $f$ be real-valued on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The formal statement assumes a convergent power series on a ball of positive radius around $a$, zero gradient there, and a positive definite Hessian. It concludes a local minimum. Its proof obtains smoothness from the power series before applying the remainder argument.
notes.second_derivative_test_analyticAt: Let $f$ be real-valued on a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The formal statement assumes that $f$ is analytic at $a$, that $\nabla f(a)=0$, and that $D^2f(a)[h,h]>0$ whenever $h\ne0$. It concludes $f(a)\le f(x)$ throughout some neighbourhood of $a$. The conclusion does not include strictness or an explicit neighbourhood size.
